tasks.q: A developer edits total = price * quantity. What are they editing?
a: Source code
A processor circuit
The finished machine-code executable
A RAM address
tasks.fb: The expression is human-readable source code. It describes a calculation without listing individual processor operations.

tasks.q: What can a processor execute directly?
a: Machine-code instructions for its instruction set
Any English instruction
Python source without any translator
Comments in a source file
tasks.fb: The processor recognises its machine-code instruction set. It does not directly understand high-level source.

opts: A requirement to manage every register
tasks.fb: Clear source makes the intention easier to follow. Binary and register management add detail for the programmer.

tasks.q: A statement calculates the average of three readings. How many machine instructions must it become?
a: The number depends on the language implementation and target processor
Exactly one in every case
Always exactly three
None, because high-level code bypasses the CPU
tasks.fb: A high-level operation can become several low-level instructions; the mapping is not a fixed universal ratio.

items: Instructions are closely tied to one processor family
Code focuses on the problem rather than each CPU step
tasks.fb: Both levels are useful. Choose according to the problem and the control needed.

tasks.q: Which is a realistic drawback of low-level programming?
a: It takes specialist knowledge and is harder to move between processor families
It can never access hardware
It is automatically free of bugs
It cannot contain instructions
tasks.fb: Detailed control brings more work for the programmer and stronger dependence on the target architecture.

tasks.q: A program must run on several types of computer. Which choice usually helps?
a: High-level source with compatible tools for each target
Machine code for just one CPU used unchanged everywhere
Removing every translator
Using memory addresses as all variable names
tasks.fb: High-level source generally travels more easily, but platform-specific libraries or features can still require changes.

tasks.q: Why might an executable made for one processor fail on another?
a: The target processor may use a different instruction set
The source uses too many comments
All executables require the original editor
Executables contain no instructions
tasks.fb: Compiled code must match the required target platform.

tasks.q: Choose a language level and the reason that best meets the museum brief.

a: High-level source makes regular feature changes easier for a team to maintain
High-level is always faster because it is newer
Assembly is best because it is harder to read
Machine code works unchanged on all processors
tasks.fb: A justified choice connects a characteristic to the particular project, rather than making an absolute claim.

tasks.q: Now choose for a carefully specified hardware-control routine.
A program is readable and compiles successfully. What must the developer still do?
a: Test that the outputs meet the requirements
Assume every result is correct
Delete the test data
Convert the source to a picture
tasks.fb: Translation can succeed even when a program implements the wrong calculation.

tasks.q: A team must maintain a timetable app across different systems. Which recommendation is best justified?
a: High-level source for maintainability and portability, with compatible tools on each system
Machine code because one binary fits every CPU
Assembly because no specialist knowledge is needed
No programming language is needed
tasks.fb: Link the choice to the team and target platforms. Portability still has conditions.

tasks.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Instructions executed directly by the target CPU
Ease of moving a program between systems
tasks.fb: Source code is translated or processed for execution; machine code is specific to the target instruction set.

info.title: Instructions for people and processors
info.text: Source code is the version a programmer writes and edits. A processor executes instructions in its own machine code. High-level source must be processed by a suitable translator before the processor can perform its instructions. Think: Why can a processor not directly execute a Python assignment as written?

info.title: High-level languages
info.text: High-level languages hide many hardware details. Meaningful names and familiar expressions help people write, read and maintain code. One high-level statement can require several machine instructions. Think: Why could a high-level language reduce the time spent maintaining a school booking system?

info.title: Low-level languages
info.text: Machine code and assembly language are low-level forms. Assembly uses mnemonic instruction names rather than long strings of binary. Low-level code is closely tied to a processor instruction set and exposes hardware details. Think: Why might low-level code be useful in a small part of a device controller?

info.title: Portability is conditional
info.text: High-level source is usually easier to move between platforms. The destination still needs a compatible implementation and required libraries. A compiled executable normally targets a particular platform; portable source does not make every executable universal. Think: A source file runs on two systems after installing compatible tools. Does this prove one compiled executable will run everywhere?

info.title: Choose for the brief
info.text: There is no best language level for every project. Compare development time, maintenance, portability and hardware control. Support a recommendation with the needs stated in the brief. Think: Recommend a level for a museum booking tool used on several systems. Link your choice to two needs.

info.title: Challenge the shortcuts
info.text: Readable code can still contain errors. Low-level code is not automatically faster than every compiled high-level program. Testing checks behaviour; choosing a language does not prove correctness. Think: Explain why “low-level always means faster” is too strong.
